He climbed onto the spirited horse that had carried him to victory in Greece. He rode until the exhausting exercise dulled his senses, burying his troubled thoughts in physical sensation.

Slowly, he regained control of himself. At last, like someone recovering from poison, he raised his head above the fever and passion into the quiet air of clear thought. He considered what he should do. First he was struck by how much time had passed while madness, rather than reason, had governed his actions. A month had gone by, and he had not seen Evadne in all that time. Her hold over him, rooted in few of his lasting feelings, had weakened greatly. He was no longer her slave or her lover. He would never see her again, and by returning completely to Perdita, he would earn her trust.

Yet as he made this decision, his imagination brought back the Greek girl's miserable home. She had refused, out of noble principle, to exchange it for a more comfortable one. He remembered the grandeur of her position and appearance when they first met. He thought of her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every luxury of the East, and of her poverty now: her daily work, her loneliness, her pale cheeks marked by hunger. Pity filled his heart. He would see her once more and find some way to restore her place in society and the benefits of her rank. Then their separation would follow naturally.

He also remembered how, throughout that long month, he had avoided Perdita, running from her as though from his own guilty conscience. But now he had come to his senses. He would put everything right, and his future devotion would erase the memory of this single stain on their peaceful life. The thought cheered him, and he calmly and firmly planned his actions. He remembered promising Perdita that he would attend a celebration in his honour that very evening, October 19, the anniversary of his election as Protector. The celebration would be a good sign for their happiness in the coming years. First, he would call briefly on Evadne. He would not stay, but he owed her an explanation and some attempt to make up for his long, unexplained absence. Then he would return to Perdita and the world he had forgotten: his social duties, the splendour of his position, and the pleasures of power.

After the scene described in the preceding pages, Perdita had expected a complete change in Raymond's behaviour. She had looked forward to speaking openly together again, and to the return of the affectionate companionship that had made her life so happy.

A few days later, Virginia and her curly-headed cavalier rode out over Brockley meadows. In passing through a hedge she tore her riding habit so badly that, on reaching home, she decided to use the back stairs and avoid being seen. Hurrying past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door stood open, she thought she noticed somebody within. Supposing it to be her mother's maid, who occasionally brought her sewing there, she peered inside to ask for help mending her habit. To her great astonishment, it was the Canterville Ghost himself! He sat beside the window, observing the broken gold of the yellowing trees drifting through the air and the red leaves whirling wildly along the avenue. His head rested upon one hand, and every part of his posture expressed profound dejection. Indeed, he seemed so desolate and so badly in need of repair that little Virginia, whose first impulse had been to flee and shut herself into her room, felt a rush of compassion and resolved to offer him comfort. Her steps were so soft, and his sadness so consuming, that he did not notice her until she addressed him.

‘I feel so sorry for you,’ she said, ‘but my brothers return to Eton tomorrow, and after that nobody will trouble you, provided you behave.’

‘Asking me to behave is ridiculous,’ he replied, turning in surprise toward the pretty little girl who had dared speak to him. ‘Perfectly ridiculous. I have to shake my chains, moan through keyholes, and wander about at night, if those are the things you mean. They are my sole purpose in existing.’

‘That is no purpose at all, and you know you have been terribly wicked. On the very day we arrived, Mrs. Umney told us you murdered your wife.’

‘Well, I admit that entirely,’ said the Ghost peevishly, ‘but it was strictly a family affair, and nobody else's concern.’

‘Killing anyone is very wrong,’ Virginia answered, with the gentle Puritan solemnity she sometimes inherited from an old New England ancestor.

‘Oh, how I detest the facile harshness of abstract morality! My wife was extremely plain, never saw that my ruffs were properly starched, and understood nothing of cooking. Why, once I shot a buck in Hogley Woods, a splendid pricket, and can you imagine how she had it served? Still, that hardly matters now; it is all finished. And even though I killed her, I do not consider it particularly kind of her brothers to have starved me to death.’

If, however, you want one for use here at home, I can provide an excellent item and guarantee you will be pleased with the result. May I ask who it is for? If the recipient is a policeman or anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I am afraid I cannot help. English detectives are really our greatest friends. I have always found that, by depending on their stupidity, we can do exactly as we please. I could not afford to lose a single one.’

‘I assure you,’ Lord Arthur said, ‘this has absolutely nothing to do with the police. The clock is actually intended for the Dean of Chichester.’

‘Good heavens! I had no idea you held such strong views on religion, Lord Arthur. Very few young men do these days.’

‘I'm afraid you give me too much credit, Herr Winckelkopf,’ Lord Arthur replied, blushing. ‘The truth is, I know practically nothing about theology.’

‘Then it is an entirely private affair?’

‘Entirely private.’

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room. A few minutes later he returned carrying a round piece of dynamite about the size of a penny and a pretty little French clock. On top stood a gilded bronze figure of Liberty crushing the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur's face lit up at the sight. ‘That is exactly what I need,’ he exclaimed. ‘Now tell me how it goes off.’

‘Ah, that is my secret,’ Herr Winckelkopf answered, regarding his invention with understandable pride. ‘Tell me when you want it to explode, and I will set the mechanism to that precise moment.’

‘Well, today is Tuesday. If you could send it immediately—’

‘That is impossible. I have a great deal of important work to do for some friends in Moscow. I might be able to send it tomorrow, though.’

‘That will be quite soon enough,’ Lord Arthur said politely, ‘provided it arrives tomorrow night or Thursday morning. As for the explosion, let's say Friday at exactly noon. The Dean is always at home then.’

‘Friday at noon,’ Herr Winckelkopf repeated, noting the instruction in a large ledger on a desk near the fireplace.

‘And now,’ said Lord Arthur, getting to his feet, ‘please tell me how much I owe you.’

‘It is such a small job, Lord Arthur, that I would rather not charge for it. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock is three pounds ten, and delivery will be about five shillings. I am delighted to help any friend of Count Rouvaloff.’

‘But what about your time and effort, Herr Winckelkopf?’
